newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official takes indirect slap at Sunbeam cuts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official takes indirect slap at Sunbeam cuts.

text.p: Outgoing Labor Secretary Robert Reich verbally slapped Sunbeam Corp. Chairman Albert Dunlap Wednesday for cutting half the company's work force, though he steered clear of singling out Dunlap or the company.

In a farewell address to Labor Department staffers, Reich contrasted his own method of shrinking his agency without layoffs with that of Dunlap, known as "Chainsaw Al," whose approach to corporate restructuring represents all that Reich has railed against the past four years.

"I'm not going to make any comment about a major company that just laid off ... half its workers over the last couple of days," Reich said as part of lengthy response to a staffer who expressed concern about job security at the agency.

"I'm not going to say that that's irresponsible corporate behavior," he said wryly, drawing a laugh from the assembled staffers. "It would be inappropriate and presumptuous of me to make that comment. And so I will not say that."

Four months after Dunlap took over at Sunbeam, the ailing appliance maker said Tuesday it would cut 6,000 jobs -- half its work force -- eliminate 87 percent of its product lines and reduce the number of its facilities to 14 from 53.

As chairman of Scott Paper Co., Dunlap was credited with turning the company around by firing 10,000 workers and selling more than $2 billion of assets before it was sold to Kimberly-Clark in December. For his 18 months of work at Scott Paper, Dunlap was paid $100 million.
After leaving Scott Paper in December, Dunlap completed his autobiography, "Mean Business: How I Save Bad Companies and Make Good Companies Great."

Reich made his comments after describing the Labor Department's job cuts. The work force was pared to 16,600 from 18,540 in 1992 through attrition and redeployment of staffers and re-engineering rather than layoffs, he said.

"And it seems to me that that is a good management practice," he said. "That is a wise management practice. It is also possible for us through re-invention to do more for the American people even though we are downsizing. That is a good management practice."
Asked about Sunbeam later in a television interview, Reich still declined to single out the company, but said firms should take a longer-term, more humane approach to downsizing.

"If you are trying to build a company that builds loyalty, expertise, skill and everything else, you've got to look five years out; you've got to take a much longer approach," Reich said on CNBC television.
"The stock price might go up in the short term, but in the long term if you do not have loyal and committed workers you are not going to show profits on the bottom line," he said.

Reich, who has announced his departure from the Clinton administration, has verbally spared with Dunlap on television. A favorite phrase of his has been that companies should regard employees "as assets to be developed, not as costs to be cut."

In his warm and fuzzy appearance before Labor Department staffers, he said he told President Clinton that he would be willing to remain on the job through inauguration day on Jan. 20 if necessary, before returning to his family in Massachusetts.
"The president would like to name a successor before Jan. 20, before I leave," he said. "I'm going to aim for that, the president is going to aim for that, but obviously we just can't guarantee it."
